items.readable_text:
Content:
In this lesson, we'll explore how to find the area of an arbitrary triangle in the coordinate plane.

Content:
Consider [MATH: \triangle ABC] with vertices

Content:
[MATH: A(2,3), \qquad
B(6,7), \qquad
C(8,2),]

Content:
as shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/281974827fbbbb46a0f872e1050dd93d]

Content:
Finding the area of this triangle using the usual methods is tricky because it's not easy to determine the length of the perpendicular height to a given base. So instead, we will proceed using an indirect method.

Content:
First, we notice that we can inscribe our triangle within the rectangle shown in the diagram below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/fa7e4ab3f6de8bb845f934f73c6e3eb0]

Content:
Inscribing a triangle in a rectangle means drawing a rectangle around the triangle in such a way that the triangle lies completely inside the rectangle and each of the triangles vertices touches the rectangle.

Content:
We have the rectangle, whose area we denote by [MATH: A_{\square},] and four triangles:

Content:
- [MATH: \triangle ABC,] whose area [MATH: A_{\triangle}] we're required to determine,
- the right triangle with hypotenuse [MATH: \overline{AB}] and area that we denote by [MATH: A_1,]
- the right triangle with hypotenuse [MATH: \overline{BC}] and area that we denote by [MATH: A_2,]
- the right triangle with hypotenuse [MATH: \overline{AC}] and area that we denote by [MATH: A_3.]

Content:
Recall that the area of a figure consisting of several smaller non-overlapping parts is equal to the sum of the areas of those parts. So, we have

Content:
[MATH: A_{\square} = A_{\triangle} + A_1 + A_2 + A_3]
which means that

Content:
[MATH: A_{\triangle} = A_{\square} - A_1 - A_2 - A_3.]

Content:
In other words, the area of the required (blue) triangle equals the area of the orange rectangle minus the areas of the three triangles with areas [MATH: A_1, A_2,] and [MATH: A_3.] Notice that it's much easier to find the areas of these three triangles compared to the blue triangle, since their bases and heights are easily determined from the diagram.

Content:
Let's now compute all the areas on the right-hand side of this equation.

Content:
- For the area of the rectangle, we have
[MATH: A_{◻}|= width ⋅ height; = 6 ⋅ 5; = 30.]
- For the area of the right triangle with hypotenuse [MATH: \overline{AB},] we have
[MATH: A_{1}|= (1)/(2) ⋅ leg_{1} ⋅ leg_{2}; = (1)/(2) ⋅ 4 ⋅ 4; = 8.]
- For the area of the right triangle with hypotenuse [MATH: \overline{BC},] we have
[MATH: A_{2}|= (1)/(2) ⋅ leg_{1} ⋅ leg_{2}; = (1)/(2) ⋅ 2 ⋅ 5; = 5.]
- For the area of the right triangle with hypotenuse [MATH: \overline{AC},] we have
[MATH: A_{3}|= (1)/(2) ⋅ leg_{1} ⋅ leg_{2}; = (1)/(2) ⋅ 6 ⋅ 1; = 3.]

Content:
Therefore, the area of [MATH: \triangle ABC] is

Content:
[MATH: A_{\triangle} = 30 - 8 - 5 - 3 = 14]

Content:
square units.

sections.normalized_html: The triangle [MATH: \triangle ABC] is inscribed in a rectangle as depicted on the diagram above. Find the area of [MATH: \triangle ABC.]
sections.readable_text:
[IMG: /graphics/e2ad9772753c0babe9352f43bb41bbd5]

The triangle [MATH: \triangle ABC] is inscribed in a rectangle as depicted on the diagram above. Find the area of [MATH: \triangle ABC.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
We have the rectangle, whose area we denote by [MATH: A_{\square},] and four triangles:

  • [MATH: \triangle ABC,] whose area [MATH: A_{\triangle}] we're required to determine,

  • the right triangle with hypotenuse [MATH: \overline{AB}] and area [MATH: A_1,]

  • the right triangle with hypotenuse [MATH: \overline{BC}] and area [MATH: A_2,]

  • the right triangle with hypotenuse [MATH: \overline{AC}] and area [MATH: A_3.]

Recall that the area of a figure consisting of several smaller non-overlapping parts is equal to the sum of the areas of those parts. So, we have

[MATH: A_{\square} = A_{\triangle} + A_1 + A_2 + A_3] which means that

[MATH: A_{\triangle} = A_{\square} - A_1 - A_2 - A_3.]

Let's now compute all the areas on the right-hand side of this equation.

  • For the area of the rectangle, we have [MATH: A_{◻}|= width ⋅ height; = 9 ⋅ 6; = 54cm^{2}.]

  • For the area of the right triangle with hypotenuse [MATH: \overline{AB},] we have [MATH: A_{1}|= (1)/(2) ⋅ leg_{1} ⋅ leg_{2}; = (1)/(2) ⋅ 9 ⋅ 3; = 13.5cm^{2}.]

  • For the area of the right triangle with hypotenuse [MATH: \overline{BC},] we have [MATH: A_{2}|= (1)/(2) ⋅ leg_{1} ⋅ leg_{2}; = (1)/(2) ⋅ 6 ⋅ 3; = 9cm^{2}.]

  • For the area of the right triangle with hypotenuse [MATH: \overline{AC},] we have [MATH: A_{3}|= (1)/(2) ⋅ leg_{1} ⋅ leg_{2}; = (1)/(2) ⋅ 3 ⋅ 6; = 9cm^{2}.]

Therefore, the area of [MATH: \triangle ABC] is

[MATH: A_{\triangle} = 54 - 13.5 - 9 - 9 = 22.5 \: \text{cm}^2.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
In this lesson, we'll explore how to find the area of an arbitrary triangle in the coordinate plane.

Content:
Consider [MATH: \triangle ABC] with vertices

Content:
[MATH: A(2,3), \qquad
B(6,7), \qquad
C(8,2),]

Content:
as shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/281974827fbbbb46a0f872e1050dd93d]

Content:
Finding the area of this triangle using the usual methods is tricky because it's not easy to determine the length of the perpendicular height to a given base. So instead, we will proceed using an indirect method.

Content:
First, we notice that we can inscribe our triangle within the rectangle shown in the diagram below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/fa7e4ab3f6de8bb845f934f73c6e3eb0]

Content:
Inscribing a triangle in a rectangle means drawing a rectangle around the triangle in such a way that the triangle lies completely inside the rectangle and each of the triangles vertices touches the rectangle.

Content:
We have the rectangle, whose area we denote by [MATH: A_{\square},] and four triangles:

Content:
- [MATH: \triangle ABC,] whose area [MATH: A_{\triangle}] we're required to determine,
- the right triangle with hypotenuse [MATH: \overline{AB}] and area that we denote by [MATH: A_1,]
- the right triangle with hypotenuse [MATH: \overline{BC}] and area that we denote by [MATH: A_2,]
- the right triangle with hypotenuse [MATH: \overline{AC}] and area that we denote by [MATH: A_3.]

Content:
Recall that the area of a figure consisting of several smaller non-overlapping parts is equal to the sum of the areas of those parts. So, we have

Content:
[MATH: A_{\square} = A_{\triangle} + A_1 + A_2 + A_3]
which means that

Content:
[MATH: A_{\triangle} = A_{\square} - A_1 - A_2 - A_3.]

Content:
In other words, the area of the required (blue) triangle equals the area of the orange rectangle minus the areas of the three triangles with areas [MATH: A_1, A_2,] and [MATH: A_3.] Notice that it's much easier to find the areas of these three triangles compared to the blue triangle, since their bases and heights are easily determined from the diagram.

Content:
Let's now compute all the areas on the right-hand side of this equation.

Content:
- For the area of the rectangle, we have
[MATH: A_{◻}|= width ⋅ height; = 6 ⋅ 5; = 30.]
- For the area of the right triangle with hypotenuse [MATH: \overline{AB},] we have
[MATH: A_{1}|= (1)/(2) ⋅ leg_{1} ⋅ leg_{2}; = (1)/(2) ⋅ 4 ⋅ 4; = 8.]
- For the area of the right triangle with hypotenuse [MATH: \overline{BC},] we have
[MATH: A_{2}|= (1)/(2) ⋅ leg_{1} ⋅ leg_{2}; = (1)/(2) ⋅ 2 ⋅ 5; = 5.]
- For the area of the right triangle with hypotenuse [MATH: \overline{AC},] we have
[MATH: A_{3}|= (1)/(2) ⋅ leg_{1} ⋅ leg_{2}; = (1)/(2) ⋅ 6 ⋅ 1; = 3.]

Content:
Therefore, the area of [MATH: \triangle ABC] is

Content:
[MATH: A_{\triangle} = 30 - 8 - 5 - 3 = 14]

Content:
square units.

Item 2 — Example: Finding the Area of a Triangle Inscribed in a Rectangle

Example Prompt:
[IMG: /graphics/e2ad9772753c0babe9352f43bb41bbd5]

The triangle [MATH: \triangle ABC] is inscribed in a rectangle as depicted on the diagram above. Find the area of [MATH: \triangle ABC.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
[IMG: /graphics/885847c9f0cfa73d7006b794abf3fca7]

We have the rectangle, whose area we denote by [MATH: A_{\square},] and four triangles:

- [MATH: \triangle ABC,] whose area [MATH: A_{\triangle}] we're required to determine,
- the right triangle with hypotenuse [MATH: \overline{AB}] and area [MATH: A_1,]
- the right triangle with hypotenuse [MATH: \overline{BC}] and area [MATH: A_2,]
- the right triangle with hypotenuse [MATH: \overline{AC}] and area [MATH: A_3.]

Recall that the area of a figure consisting of several smaller non-overlapping parts is equal to the sum of the areas of those parts. So, we have

[MATH: A_{\square} = A_{\triangle} + A_1 + A_2 + A_3]
which means that

[MATH: A_{\triangle} = A_{\square} - A_1 - A_2 - A_3.]

Let's now compute all the areas on the right-hand side of this equation.

- For the area of the rectangle, we have
[MATH: A_{◻}|= width ⋅ height; = 9 ⋅ 6; = 54cm^{2}.]
- For the area of the right triangle with hypotenuse [MATH: \overline{AB},] we have
[MATH: A_{1}|= (1)/(2) ⋅ leg_{1} ⋅ leg_{2}; = (1)/(2) ⋅ 9 ⋅ 3; = 13.5cm^{2}.]
- For the area of the right triangle with hypotenuse [MATH: \overline{BC},] we have
[MATH: A_{2}|= (1)/(2) ⋅ leg_{1} ⋅ leg_{2}; = (1)/(2) ⋅ 6 ⋅ 3; = 9cm^{2}.]
- For the area of the right triangle with hypotenuse [MATH: \overline{AC},] we have
[MATH: A_{3}|= (1)/(2) ⋅ leg_{1} ⋅ leg_{2}; = (1)/(2) ⋅ 3 ⋅ 6; = 9cm^{2}.]

Therefore, the area of [MATH: \triangle ABC] is

[MATH: A_{\triangle} = 54 - 13.5 - 9 - 9 = 22.5 \: \text{cm}^2.]

Item 5 — Example: Finding the Area of a Triangle in the Coordinate Plane

Example Prompt:
Find the area of the triangle with vertices [MATH: (-4,3),] [MATH: (2,5),] and [MATH: (-1,-2).]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, note that we can inscribe our triangle within the rectangle shown in the diagram below.

[IMG: /graphics/c0d64b054cfb3309e57590280580427a]

We have the rectangle, whose area we denote by [MATH: A_{\square},] and four triangles:

- [MATH: \triangle ABC,] whose area [MATH: A_{\triangle}] we're required to determine,
- the right triangle with hypotenuse [MATH: \overline{AB}] and area [MATH: A_1,]
- the right triangle with hypotenuse [MATH: \overline{BC}] and area [MATH: A_2,]
- the right triangle with hypotenuse [MATH: \overline{AC}] and area [MATH: A_3.]

Recall that the area of a figure consisting of several smaller non-overlapping parts is equal to the sum of the areas of those parts. So, we have

[MATH: A_{\square} = A_{\triangle} + A_1 + A_2 + A_3]

which means that

[MATH: A_{\triangle} = A_{\square} - A_1 - A_2 - A_3.]

Let's now compute all the areas on the right-hand side of this equation.

- For the area of the rectangle, we have
[MATH: A_{◻}|= width ⋅ height; = 6 ⋅ 7; = 42.]
- For the area of the right triangle with hypotenuse [MATH: \overline{AB},] we have
[MATH: A_{1}|= (1)/(2) ⋅ leg_{1} ⋅ leg_{2}; = (1)/(2) ⋅ 6 ⋅ 2; = 6.]
- For the area of the right triangle with hypotenuse [MATH: \overline{BC},] we have
[MATH: A_{2}|= (1)/(2) ⋅ leg_{1} ⋅ leg_{2}; = (1)/(2) ⋅ 3 ⋅ 7; = 10.5.]
- For the area of the right triangle with hypotenuse [MATH: \overline{AC},] we have
[MATH: A_{3}|= (1)/(2) ⋅ leg_{1} ⋅ leg_{2}; = (1)/(2) ⋅ 3 ⋅ 5; = 7.5.]

Therefore, the area of [MATH: \triangle ABC] is
[MATH: A_{\triangle} = 42 - 6 - 10.5 - 7.5 = 18]

square units.
